content: Patients undergoing hemodialysis before the COVID-19 pandemic faced significantly higher mortality rates from COVID-19 compared to the general population. One of the primary reasons for this increased mortality is the advanced age of many dialysis patients. It is essential to implement effective measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 among this vulnerable group. Pathophysiology Patients on hemodialysis often experience a milder clinical course of COVID-19, which may be attributed to several factors: Individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) or end-stage renal disease (ESRD) have compromised immune systems. This reduced immunity leads to a less intense cytokine storm in response to viral antigens. Consequently, these patients rarely present with the full clinical picture of pneumonia. Hypercoagulation plays a critical role in worsening the disease. It triggers the coagulation cascade, leading to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), which results in organ dysfunction and increased mortality in COVID-19 patients. However, the use of anticoagulants during hemodialysis helps inhibit the coagulation cascade, thereby preventing hypercoagulation and DIC. A study conducted at the Renmin Hospital in Wuhan revealed that, within one month, 37 out of 230 dialysis patients were infected with COVID-19, along with four healthcare staff members. Peripheral blood examinations of infected dialysis patients showed reduced levels of killer T cells, helper T cells, natural killer cells, and lower levels of inflammatory cytokines compared to non-dialysis COVID-19 patients. Epidemiology and Demographics Patients on maintenance hemodialysis and those with ESRD are at an increased risk of contracting COVID-19 due to their low immunity and multiple co-morbidities. A case series involving 5,700 COVID-19 patients across 12 hospitals in the Northwell Health system in New York found that 5% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients had ESRD. The average age of dialysis patients was between 70 and 90 years, compared to 20 to 60 years in the general population. A study conducted in 208 acute care hospitals in the UK, involving 20,133 patients, identified chronic kidney disease as one of the most common co-morbidities in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, present in 16% of cases. Research by Alberici et al. at four outpatient dialysis facilities in Italy reported a high overall mortality rate of 29% among dialysis patients. Treatment and Preventive Measures for COVID-19 in Hemodialysis Patients Screening of Patients Patients should be screened for COVID-19 symptoms before undergoing dialysis. The most effective approach is to contact patients in advance and inquire about symptoms. Patients reporting illness or symptoms should be placed in a designated screening area. Hand sanitizers and face masks should be provided to them. Dialysis facilities should implement a triage protocol to direct patients to testing clinics, specific dialysis facilities, or hospitals as needed. Managing Patients with Suspected Illness If hospital resources allow, patients should undergo dialysis during a specific shift or in a separate isolation dialysis ward. Patients should be instructed to wear masks and cover their mouths and noses while coughing or sneezing to reduce airborne droplet transmission. Suspected COVID-19 patients should maintain a minimum distance of 6 feet (2 meters) from others in all directions. Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) A designated group of healthcare personnel should be assigned to care for suspected COVID-19 patients. Both patients and healthcare workers should be provided with appropriate PPE. Healthcare workers should adhere to droplet and contact precautions, wearing masks, gowns, goggles, face shields, and gloves. Surgical masks and N95 respirators are recommended. Eye shields and goggles should be used to prevent droplet transmission through the eyes. Disinfection Personnel responsible for disinfection should wear PPE while cleaning dialysis surfaces. Dialysis machines, chairs, blood pressure cuffs, stethoscopes, and other equipment should be cleaned with disinfecting wipes and allowed to air dry. Optimal Resource Utilization Given the prolonged nature of the pandemic, resources should be utilized efficiently. Ideally, both healthcare workers and patients should wear gowns. If gowns are limited, healthcare workers should prioritize wearing them during critical tasks such as initiating and terminating dialysis, handling catheters and access sites, disinfecting dialysis stations, and assisting patients to and from the dialysis station. Goggles and eye shields can be reused after proper disinfection. Face masks and eye shields should be used for extended periods when necessary. A record of PPE stock should be maintained to ensure availability. Workforce Management Healthcare workers are at risk of COVID-19 infection due to exposure. To minimize this risk, staff should work in shifts. During the pandemic, healthcare workers may fall ill, leading to staff shortages. To address this, a backup list of personnel should be prepared to fill vacant positions. Training courses should be conducted to equip healthcare staff with the necessary skills to manage the situation effectively.
